questions.question: $\ce{H2O}$ (ice) is an example of
questions.answer:
**(B)** Hydrogen bonded molecular solid

In ice each H$_2$O molecule is joined to four neighbours by hydrogen bonds in a tetrahedral array, giving an open, low-density (0.917 g cm$^{-3}$) solid. The molecules are held as molecules — there are no ions — so ice is a **molecular** solid, and the force responsible for holding the lattice together is the **hydrogen bond**, not merely the dipole–dipole force of an ordinary polar molecular solid. This is why ice melts at 273 K rather than far below, and why it floats on water.

questions.question: Rate = k[H$_2$O$_2$] is an example of
questions.answer:
**(B)** first order reaction

The rate law contains the concentration of one species raised to the first power, so the reaction is **first order** — the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide,

$$\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$$

proceeds at a rate proportional to $[\ce{H2O2}]$, with $t_{1/2}=0.693/k$ independent of concentration. Note that the stoichiometric coefficient 2 does not appear in the rate law; order must never be read off a balanced equation.

questions.question: CH$_3$Br + 2Na + CH$_3$Br $\xrightarrow{\text{Dry ether}}$ CH$_3$-CH$_3$ + 2NaBr. The reaction is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Wurtz reaction

Two molecules of an alkyl halide are coupled by sodium in dry ether, the metal supplying the electrons and the halogen being removed as NaBr:

$$\ce{2CH3Br + 2Na ->[\text{dry ether}] CH3-CH3 + 2NaBr}$$

This is the **Wurtz reaction**, the standard way of doubling the carbon chain symmetrically. (The Fittig reaction is the same coupling using **aryl** halides; Friedel-Crafts is an electrophilic substitution on an arene.)

questions.question: Calamine is an ore of
questions.answer:
**(A)** Zn

**Calamine** is zinc carbonate, **$\ce{ZnCO3}$**, an important ore of zinc (also written $\ce{ZnCO3}$·$\ce{Zn(OH)2}$ as hemimorphite in some texts). It is first **calcined** to the oxide and then reduced:

$$\ce{ZnCO3 ->[\Delta] ZnO + CO2}$$

$$\ce{ZnO + C -> Zn + CO}$$

Zinc is then purified by distillation or electrolysis. (Others: zinc blende ZnS, zincite ZnO.)

questions.question: Toluene $\xrightarrow{Cl_2/h\nu}$ A; 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(D)** none of these

Under **light** the reaction is a free-radical **side-chain** substitution: light dissociates Cl$_2$ into chlorine atoms, which abstract a hydrogen from the methyl group to give the resonance-stabilised benzyl radical, and that combines with Cl$_2$ to give **benzyl chloride**:

$$\ce{C6H5CH3 + Cl2 ->[h\nu] C6H5CH2Cl + HCl}$$

So the product is benzyl chloride (further chlorination gives $\ce{C6H5CHCl2}$ and then $\ce{C6H5CCl3}$) — none of the three named compounds. *(Note on the printed key: it marks (c) chlorobenzene, which would need ring substitution; the ring is attacked only in the dark with a Lewis-acid catalyst, e.g. $\ce{Cl2/AlCl3}$, and even then the product is chlorotoluene.)*

questions.question: Acetaldehyde + 4[H] $\xrightarrow{Zn-Hg/HCl}$ A; 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Ethane

Zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid (**Clemmensen reduction**) reduces the carbonyl group of an aldehyde all the way to a $\ce{-CH3}$ group:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + 4[H] ->[Zn-Hg/HCl] CH3-CH3 + H2O}$$

So acetaldehyde gives **ethane**. The reagent works in strongly acidic solution, which is why it complements the Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazine, alkaline) for acid-sensitive compounds.

questions.question: Which enzyme helps in converting sucrose into glucose and fructose?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Invertase

**Invertase** ($\beta$-fructofuranosidase) hydrolyses the $\alpha$-1,2 glycosidic bond of sucrose:

$$\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[\text{invertase}] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$$

giving an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose. The mixture is called **invert sugar** because the optical rotation changes from dextro (+) to laevo (−) as the strongly laevorotatory fructose is set free. (Lactase acts on lactose, giving glucose + galactose; urease hydrolyses urea.)

questions.question: CH$_3$COOH + SOCl$_2$ → Product. The product is
questions.answer:
**(A)** CH$_3$COCl

Thionyl chloride converts a carboxylic acid into its **acid chloride**:

$$\ce{CH3COOH + SOCl2 -> CH3COCl + SO2 ^ + HCl ^}$$

The by-products are gases, so the acid chloride is obtained pure — this is why SOCl$_2$ (the 'Darzen's reagent' for this purpose) is preferred over PCl$_5$. The product, acetyl chloride, is a fuming liquid used for acetylation.

questions.question: Calculate the overall order of a reaction which has the rate expression Rate = k[A]$^1$[B]$^1$
questions.answer:
The overall order is the sum of the exponents in the rate law:

$$\text{order}=1+1=2$$

The reaction is **second order overall** — first order with respect to A and first order with respect to B. Its rate constant has units mol$^{-1}$ L s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Beri-beri occurs due to the deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.answer: **Vitamin B$_1$ (thiamine).** Beri-beri is a deficiency disease marked by loss of appetite, weakness, and nerve degeneration (dry beri-beri) or heart failure and oedema (wet beri-beri). Thiamine is the precursor of thiamine pyrophosphate, the coenzyme for the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate and $\alpha$-ketoglutarate, so its lack blocks carbohydrate metabolism in nerves and heart muscle. *(The printed key writes only 'Vitamin B'; the specific vitamin is B$_1$.)*

questions.question: Write dispersed phase and dispersion medium of milk, a colloidal solution.
questions.answer:
In milk the **dispersed phase is fat (a liquid)** and the **dispersion medium is water** — so milk is a **liquid-in-liquid (emulsion) colloid**, specifically an oil-in-water emulsion stabilised by the milk protein casein.

The fat globules are of colloidal size (about 1–10 $\mu$m) and carry a negative charge from the adsorbed protein, which keeps them apart. Creaming (separation of the fat) is prevented by homogenisation, which reduces the globule size.

questions.question: Write the monomer used for getting the polymer Glyptal.
questions.answer:
The monomers of **Glyptal** are **phthalic acid** (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid) and **ethylene glycol** (ethane-1,2-diol):

$$\ce{nC6H4(COOH)2 + nHOCH2CH2OH -> Glyptal + 2nH2O}$$

It is a **polyester** formed by condensation polymerisation, a cross-linked thermosetting resin used in paints, lacquers and enamels because it adheres strongly and resists chemicals. (Glycerol is used instead of ethylene glycol in the closely related alkyd resins.)

questions.question: Write IUPAC name of CH$_3$CH$_2$C(CH$_3$)(CH$_2$I)$\,$— i.e. CH$_3$CH$_2$C(CH$_3$)CH$_2$I.
questions.answer:
**1-iodo-2-methylbutane**

Expanding: $\ce{CH3-CH2-C(CH3)(CH2I)}$. Numbering must start at the end that gives the substituents the lowest locants. Starting from the CH$_2$I end, carbon 1 carries iodine and carbon 2 carries the methyl with an ethyl continuing to C-3, C-4 — a four-carbon chain:

$$\ce{I-CH2-C(CH3)(C2H5)}$$

So the name is **1-iodo-2-methylbutane**. (The printed key's '2-methyl iodobutane' gives the right structure but is not in IUPAC form.)

questions.question: Give an example of aldohexose.
questions.answer:
**Glucose** — an aldohexose, $\ce{C6H12O6}$, whose open-chain form has an aldehyde group at C-1 and five hydroxyls:

$$\ce{CH2OH-(CHOH)4-CHO}$$

Other aldohexoses are **galactose** and **mannose**. ('Aldo' refers to the aldehyde group, 'hexose' to the six carbons.) Because of the aldehyde it reduces Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, and it cyclises into a six-membered pyranose hemiacetal.

questions.question: Give an example of food preservative.
questions.answer:
**Vinegar (dilute acetic acid)** — used to preserve pickles, sauces and vegetables. Other examples: **sodium benzoate** (soft drinks), **sodium metabisulphite** (dried fruit), and **common salt or sugar** (by lowering water activity).

Preservatives act either by lowering the pH so that micro-organisms cannot multiply (vinegar) or by being taken up by the microbial cell and interfering with its metabolism (benzoate, sulphite).

questions.question: Define conductance and give its unit.
questions.answer:
**Conductance** is the reciprocal of resistance — a measure of how easily a current flows through a conductor:

$$G=\frac{1}{R}$$

Its SI unit is the **siemens (S)**, equal to the old 'mho' or **ohm$^{-1}$** ($\Omega^{-1}$). Since $G=1/R$, conductance is high when the resistance is low.

For a cell of known geometry it is related to the conductivity of the solution, $\kappa=G\,l/A=G\,G^*$, where $l/A$ is the cell constant. Unlike resistance, the conductance of an **electrolyte** rises with temperature because ions become more mobile.

questions.question: Giving examples, differentiate between roasting and calcination.
questions.answer:
| Roasting | Calcination |
|---|---|
| Heating the ore in a **regular (excess) supply of air/oxygen** | Heating the ore in the **absence or limited supply of air** |
| Used for **sulphide** ores | Used for **carbonate and hydrated oxide** ores |
| Oxidation takes place: $\ce{2ZnS + 3O2 ->[\Delta] 2ZnO + 2SO2}$ (zinc blende) | Thermal decomposition: $\ce{ZnCO3 ->[\Delta] ZnO + CO2}$ (calamine) |
| Sulphur is removed as SO$_2$ | CO$_2$ or water vapour is removed |
| Carried out at a high temperature, below the melting point | Same temperature range, to make the ore porous |

Both steps convert the ore to the **oxide**, from which the metal is then reduced. *(The printed answer's example for calcination, ZnCO$_3$, is right; roasting's example is written as 'ZnSO$_3$', a misprint for the sulphide ZnS.)*

questions.question: Write any two features that distinguish between physisorption and chemisorption.
questions.answer:
| Physisorption | Chemisorption |
|---|---|
| Weak **van der Waals** forces between adsorbate and adsorbent | Strong **chemical bond** between adsorbate and adsorbent |
| **Reversible** — the adsorbate can be removed by heating or lowering the pressure | **Irreversible** — the adsorbed species is chemically changed |
| Low heat of adsorption, 20–40 kJ mol$^{-1}$; occurs at low temperature; multilayer | High heat of adsorption, 80–240 kJ mol$^{-1}$; needs temperature and an activation energy; monolayer |
| Not specific; extent depends on the ease of liquefaction of the gas | Highly specific |

*Any two contrasted features.* Physisorption does not require activation energy; chemisorption usually does.

questions.question: What are the different oxidation states exhibited by Lanthanoids?
questions.answer:
Lanthanoids show mainly **+3**, with **+2** and **+4** for some members. The +3 state (loss of $6s^2$ and one $4f$ electron) is characteristic: all the lanthanoids form $\ce{Ln^{3+}}$ salts that are stable, and the ion is what gives them their similar chemistry.

- **+4** for those that can reach a stable $f^0$, $f^7$ or $f^{14}$ configuration: Ce(+4, $f^0$), Pr(+4), Tb(+4, $f^7$), and Dy(+4).
- **+2** for those that can reach $f^7$ or $f^{14}$: Eu(+2, $f^7$), Yb(+2, $f^{14}$), and Sm(+2).

The +2 and +4 states are therefore most common for the elements best able to reach a half-filled or completely filled f subshell — the same 'special stability' rule that makes Mn(II) ($d^5$) and Zn(II) ($d^{10}$) easy to form.

questions.question: Complete the following: (a) $\ce{XeF2 + H2 ->}$ (b) $\ce{XeF6 + 3H2O ->}$
questions.answer:
**(a)**

$$\ce{XeF2 + H2 -> Xe + 2HF}$$

Xenon difluoride is reduced to the free element by hydrogen — the Xe(II) state is unstable and strongly oxidising.

**(b)**

$$\ce{XeF6 + 3H2O -> XeO3 + 6HF}$$

Xenon hexafluoride is **hydrolysed to xenon trioxide**, a white, explosive solid in which xenon is in the +6 state. (Partial hydrolysis of XeF$_6$ gives XeOF$_4$ and XeO$_2$F$_2$; complete hydrolysis gives XeO$_3$, which on further reaction with alkali gives the xenate and perxenate salts.)

questions.question: What are the expected products of hydrolysis of Lactose?
questions.answer:
**Lactose on hydrolysis gives galactose and glucose** — one molecule of each:

$$\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[\text{lactase}] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$$

Lactose is a **disaccharide** in which $\beta$-D-galactose is joined to D-glucose by a $\beta$-1,4-glycosidic bond; it is the sugar of milk (about 5%) and is hydrolysed in the intestine by the enzyme lactase. Its absence causes lactose intolerance.

questions.question: Explain the difference between Buna-N and Buna-S.
questions.answer:
| Buna-S (SBR) | Buna-N (Nitrile rubber) |
|---|---|
| Copolymer of **1,3-butadiene and styrene** | Copolymer of **1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile** ($\ce{CH2=CHCN}$) |
| Polymerised in the presence of **sodium** as initiator (hence 'Bu-na') | Usually emulsion-polymerised with a peroxide initiator; sodium is not required |
| Excellent abrasion resistance and elasticity; used for tyres, shoe soles, belting | Outstanding resistance to **oil, petrol and other organic solvents**, and to heat; used for hoses, gaskets, fuel lines, gloves |
| Non-polar, swells in hydrocarbon oils | Polar because of the nitrile groups, which is why it resists oils |

In both, 1,4-addition through the conjugated diene gives the main chain with a double bond remaining, which is what can be vulcanised.

questions.question: Write briefly with one example on the following: (a) Analgesics (b) Antiseptic
questions.answer:
**(a) Analgesics** are drugs that **relieve pain without causing loss of consciousness** (unlike anaesthetics). They are of two kinds: **non-narcotic** (e.g. **aspirin** — also antipyretic and anti-inflammatory; paracetamol, ibuprofen), which act on the peripheral site of pain, and **narcotic** (e.g. morphine, codeine), which act on the central nervous system and can be addictive.

**(b) Antiseptics** are chemicals that **kill or inhibit micro-organisms on living tissue** — skin, wounds, mucous membranes — without damaging the tissue. Example: **Dettol (chloroxylenol)**, also savlon, bithional, and dilute (0.2–1%) phenol. They differ from disinfectants, which are too strong for living tissue and are used on inanimate objects.

questions.question: Explain ferromagnetic substance and anti-ferromagnetic substance.
questions.answer:
**Ferromagnetic substances** are those attracted very strongly by a magnetic field and which retain **permanent magnetism even when the field is removed**. In them the magnetic moments of adjacent atoms are **aligned parallel** in domains, so their effects add up: $\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow$. Example: **iron, cobalt, nickel** (and Gd). Above the Curie temperature the alignment is destroyed and they become paramagnetic.

**Anti-ferromagnetic substances** have their neighbouring magnetic moments **aligned in opposite (antiparallel) directions in equal numbers**, so the moments cancel and the substance has **no net magnetic moment** — it is only weakly affected by a field, and its susceptibility below the Néel temperature is small: $\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow$. Example: **MnO, Mn$_2$O$_3$, Cr$_2$O$_3$**.

(In between lies **ferrimagnetism**, where the antiparallel moments are unequal so a net moment survives — as in magnetite, Fe$_3$O$_4$.)

questions.question: Explain rate of chemical reaction.
questions.answer:
The **rate of a chemical reaction** is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, **divided by its stoichiometric coefficient** in the balanced equation:

$$\text{rate}=-\frac{1}{a}\frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt}=+\frac{1}{c}\frac{d[\text{C}]}{dt}$$

Reactant concentrations decrease, so a minus sign is used for them. For

$$\ce{2HI -> H2 + I2}$$

$$\text{rate}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\ce{HI}]}{dt}=\frac{d[\ce{H2}]}{dt}=\frac{d[\ce{I2}]}{dt}$$

The unit is concentration per unit time, **mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$**. The rate falls as the reaction proceeds (reactants are used up) and is strongly temperature-dependent; the **average** rate is measured over a time interval, the **instantaneous** rate is the tangent to the concentration–time curve, and the **initial** rate is evaluated at $t=0$.

questions.question: Explain the following terms: (a) Dialysis (b) Tyndall effect
questions.answer:
**(a) Dialysis.** The removal of dissolved (crystalline) impurities from a colloidal sol by means of a **semi-permeable membrane** such as parchment or cellophane. Colloidal particles are too large to pass through the pores, while ions and small molecules diffuse out into the surrounding water. The sol is taken in a parchment bag suspended in running water and the impurities slowly diffuse out, leaving a purified sol — this is how arsenious sulphide sol is freed from the electrolyte used to make it. In **electrodialysis** an electric field is applied to speed the removal of ions, which is used in artificial kidneys.

**(b) Tyndall effect.** When a **beam of light is passed through a colloidal sol**, the path of the beam becomes **visible** as a bright cone because the colloidal particles (1–1000 nm) are large enough to **scatter** the light. The illuminated path is the **Tyndall cone**. The effect is not shown by a true solution (particles too small to scatter) and is the standard optical test that distinguishes a colloid from a solution; it is what makes a sunbeam visible through a dusty room or fog.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following transformations? (a) Methyl alcohol to Methyl iodide (b) Ethyl bromide to Ethene (c) Benzyl bromide to Benzyl cyanide
questions.answer:
**(a) Methyl alcohol → methyl iodide:** nucleophilic substitution with HI (or KI + H$_3$PO$_4$):

$$\ce{CH3OH + HI -> CH3I + H2O}$$

**(b) Ethyl bromide → ethene:** dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH:

$$\ce{C2H5Br ->[KOH(alc)][\Delta] C2H4 ^ + KBr + H2O}$$

**(c) Benzyl bromide → benzyl cyanide:** nucleophilic substitution by cyanide in aqueous ethanol, which extends the chain by one carbon:

$$\ce{C6H5CH2Br + KCN ->[\text{aq. ethanol}] C6H5CH2CN + KBr}$$

The benzylic halide reacts readily by S$_N$1 (the benzylic cation is stabilised by the ring), so mild conditions suffice.

questions.question: Using IUPAC norms write formulae for the following: (a) Potassium tri(oxalato)chromate(III) (b) Tetrabromidocuprate(II) (c) Hexaamminenickel(II) chloride
questions.answer:
**(a)** Three bidentate oxalate ligands (each −2) and Cr(III): $+3+3(-2)=-3$, so the anion is $[\ce{Cr(C2O4)3}]^{3-}$ and needs three K$^+$:

$$\ce{K3[Cr(C2O4)3]}$$

**(b)** Four bromide ligands (each −1) and Cu(II): $+2+4(-1)=-2$:

$$\ce{[CuBr4]^{2-}}$$

**(c)** Six neutral NH$_3$ with Ni(II) gives a $+2$ cation, balanced by two chlorides:

$$\ce{[Ni(NH3)6]Cl2}$$

*(The printed answer for (b) writes the neutral $[\ce{CuBr4}]$; the ion carries a 2− charge, which matters because tetrabromidocuprate(II) is isolated as its potassium salt, $\ce{K2[CuBr4]}$.)*

questions.question: What are oxidation potential and reduction potential?
questions.answer:
**Oxidation potential** is the potential of an electrode at which **oxidation** (loss of electrons) takes place — i.e. the tendency of the reduced form to give up electrons and be oxidised. It is the potential of the **anode** of a cell, and is the negative of the reduction potential:

$$E_{\text{ox}}=-E_{\text{red}}$$

**Reduction potential** is the potential of an electrode at which **reduction** (gain of electrons) takes place — the tendency of the oxidised form to accept electrons. It is the potential of the **cathode** and is the quantity tabulated as the standard electrode potential $E^\circ$ (relative to the hydrogen electrode, taken as 0 V).

A larger (more positive) reduction potential means a greater tendency to be reduced, so that half-cell acts as the cathode and the other is oxidised. Both are measured under standard conditions (1 M, 1 bar, 298 K) when quoted as $E^\circ$.

questions.question: Predict the product: (a) $\ce{CH3CH2Br + KCN ->[\text{aq. ethanol}]}$ (b) $\ce{(CH3)3C-OC2H5 + HI ->}$ (c) $\ce{CH3COONa ->[NaOH][CaO,\Delta]}$
questions.answer:
**(a)** Nucleophilic substitution gives **propanenitrile** (ethyl cyanide), extending the chain by one carbon:

$$\ce{CH3CH2Br + KCN ->[\text{aq. ethanol}] CH3CH2CN + KBr}$$

**(b)** An ether is cleaved by HI. The iodide attacks the **less hindered** alkyl group in an S$_N$2 manner, so the methyl groups stay with the oxygen and the ethyl group becomes the iodide:

$$\ce{(CH3)3C-OC2H5 + HI -> (CH3)3C-OH + C2H5I}$$

i.e. **2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butanol) and iodoethane**. *(The printed answer writes ethanol + tert-butyl iodide, which is the wrong way round: with a tertiary alkyl group the $\ce{C-O}$ bond breaks on the tertiary side only if an S$_N$1 route operates; the standard rule for this ether is that I$^-$ displaces the primary ethyl group. Either way, the answer must name both fragments.)*

**(c)** Decarboxylation with soda lime gives **methane**:

$$\ce{CH3COONa + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta] CH4 ^ + Na2CO3}$$

questions.question: Complete the following reactions: (a) C + conc. HNO$_3$ (b) Sn + PCl$_5$ (c) benzene + CH$_3$COCl $\xrightarrow{AlCl_3,\text{anhydrous}}$
questions.answer:
**(a)** Carbon is oxidised to CO$_2$ by hot concentrated nitric acid, which is reduced to NO$_2$:

$$\ce{C + 4HNO3(conc.) -> CO2 ^ + 4NO2 ^ + 2H2O}$$

**(b)** Tin(IV) chloride is formed, the phosphorus being reduced to PCl$_3$:

$$\ce{Sn + 4PCl5 -> SnCl4 + 4PCl3}$$

(The printed key writes 'SnCl$_4$ + PCl', which is not a real species; PCl$_5$ is reduced to **PCl$_3$**, and four molecules are needed to supply four chlorines.)

**(c)** Friedel-Crafts acylation gives **acetophenone**:

$$\ce{C6H6 + CH3COCl ->[AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 + HCl}$$

Anhydrous conditions are essential, since water would destroy the AlCl$_3$ catalyst.

questions.question: Vapour pressure of water at 293 K is 17.535 mm Hg. Calculate the vapour pressure of water at 293 K when 25 g of glucose is dissolved in 450 g of water. / Draw the structures of the following compounds: (a) XeOF$_2$ (b) H$_3$PO$_4$ (c) H$_3$PO$_3$ (d) IF$_5$ (e) IF$_7$
questions.answer:
**Numerical.** Glucose is non-volatile and non-electrolyte, so by Raoult's law the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of solute:

$$\frac{p^\circ-p_s}{p^\circ}=\frac{n_2}{n_1+n_2}$$

with

$$n_2=\frac{25}{180}=0.1389\ \text{mol (glucose)},\qquad n_1=\frac{450}{18}=25.0\ \text{mol (water)}$$

$$\frac{p^\circ-p_s}{p^\circ}=\frac{0.1389}{25.139}=0.005525$$

$$p_s=p^\circ(1-0.005525)=17.535\times0.994475=17.44\ \text{mm Hg}$$

**The vapour pressure of the solution is 17.44 mm Hg**, a lowering of about 0.095 mm — small because the solution is dilute (glucose is only 0.55 mol %).

**Structures.**

**(a) $\ce{XeOF2}$** — xenon(IV), $sp^3d$; a **T-shaped** molecule: two F and the O around Xe with two lone pairs occupying the remaining trigonal-bipyramidal sites. (The $\ce{Xe=O}$ is a double bond.)

**(b) $\ce{H3PO4}$** — phosphorus(V), tetrahedral: one $\ce{P=O}$ and **three P–OH** groups, hence tribasic.

**(c) $\ce{H3PO3}$** — phosphorus(III), tetrahedral: one $\ce{P=O}$, **two P–OH** and **one P–H**; only the two P–OH hydrogens are acidic, so it is dibasic.

**(d) $\ce{IF5}$** — iodine(V), $sp^3d^2$; **square pyramidal** with four F in the base and one F at the apex, the lone pair occupying the sixth octahedral site.

**(e) $\ce{IF7}$** — iodine(VII), $sp^3d^3$; **pentagonal bipyramidal** with five F in a plane at 72° and one F above and below.

questions.question: Give the principle involved in the manufacture of nitric acid by Ostwald process. How does concentrated HNO$_3$ react with (i) C and (ii) I$_2$? / How does white phosphorus react with (i) H$_2$SO$_4$ (ii) sulphur (iii) Mg (iv) Na (v) HNO$_3$?
questions.answer:
**Ostwald process.** Nitric acid is made by the **catalytic oxidation of ammonia** with atmospheric oxygen over a platinum–rhodium gauze at about 800 K.

**Step 1 — oxidation of ammonia to nitric oxide:**

$$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 ->[Pt/Rh][800 K] 4NO + 6H2O}$$

**Step 2 — oxidation of NO to NO$_2$** (cooling, excess air):

$$\ce{2NO + O2 <=> 2NO2}$$

**Step 3 — absorption in water** to give nitric acid, with some NO recycled:

$$\ce{3NO2 + H2O -> 2HNO3 + NO}$$

The principle is that ammonia (N, −3) is oxidised stepwise to nitric acid (N, +5); each step is exothermic and the first is the rate-determining catalytic one, so the conditions (high pressure, cooled absorber and a platinum catalyst) are chosen to maximise both the rate and the absorption yield.

**Reaction with concentrated HNO$_3$:**

**(i) Carbon** — oxidised to CO$_2$, HNO$_3$ reduced to NO$_2$:

$$\ce{C + 4HNO3 -> CO2 ^ + 4NO2 ^ + 2H2O}$$

**(ii) Iodine** — oxidised to iodic acid:

$$\ce{I2 + 10HNO3 -> 2HIO3 + 10NO2 + 4H2O}$$

*(The printed key writes $\ce{2HIO3 + 10NO2 + 4H2O}$ correctly, but writes the equation as 'HNO$_3$ + I$_2$' unbalanced.)*

**Reactions of white phosphorus:**

**(i) With H$_2$SO$_4$:**

$$\ce{P4 + 10H2SO4 -> 4H3PO4 + 10SO2 + 4H2O}$$

(oxidised to phosphoric acid, the sulphuric acid reduced to SO$_2$).

**(ii) With sulphur:**

$$\ce{8P4 + 3S8 -> 8P4S3}$$

**(iii) With magnesium:**

$$\ce{P4 + 6Mg -> 2Mg3P2}$$

**(iv) With sodium:**

$$\ce{P4 + 12Na -> 4Na3P}$$

**(v) With nitric acid:**

$$\ce{P4 + 20HNO3 -> 4H3PO4 + 20NO2 + 4H2O}$$

In every case phosphorus is oxidised from 0 to +5 (or to the phosphide, −3, with the metals), which reflects its position as a non-metal that is easily oxidised.

questions.question: Write short notes on the following: (a) Aldol condensation (b) Sandmeyer reaction (c) Stephen reaction. / Identify 'X', 'Y' and 'Z' in the following: (a) phenol $\xrightarrow{Zn,\,\Delta}$ X′ $\xrightarrow{CH_3COCl,\,\text{anhy. }AlCl_3}$ Y′ (b) $\ce{CH3CH=CH2 ->[H3O^+]}$ X′ $\xrightarrow{K_2Cr_2O_7/H^+}$ Y′ (c) phenol + Na → X
questions.answer:
**(a) Aldol condensation.** Aldehydes and ketones having at least one **$\alpha$-hydrogen** condense in the presence of dilute alkali to give a $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone (an 'aldol'), which on heating loses water to give an $\alpha$,$\beta$-unsaturated carbonyl compound. The base removes the acidic $\alpha$-H to form a carbanion, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + CH3CHO ->[dil. NaOH] CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO ->[\Delta] CH3CH=CHCHO + H2O}$$

With propanone the product is diacetone alcohol, $\ce{(CH3)2C(OH)CH2COCH3}$.

**(b) Sandmeyer reaction.** A benzene diazonium salt is treated with a copper(I) halide in the corresponding halogen acid, and the diazonium group is replaced by the halogen:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + CuCl/HCl -> C6H5Cl + N2 ^ + CuCl2}$$

With CuBr/HBr and CuCN/KCN the products are bromobenzene and benzonitrile. It is the standard route from a primary aromatic amine to an aryl halide.

**(c) Stephen reaction.** A nitrile is reduced to an **imine hydrochloride** by tin(II) chloride and HCl gas, and the imine is hydrolysed by boiling water to the aldehyde:

$$\ce{CH3CN + SnCl2 + 2HCl -> CH3CH=NH\cdot HCl ->[H2O][\text{boil}] CH3CHO + NH4Cl}$$

It is a mild, selective way of getting an aldehyde from a nitrile without reducing it all the way to the amine (which LiAlH$_4$ would do).

**Identifications.**

**(a)** Phenol is reduced to **benzene** by zinc dust on heating; benzene then undergoes Friedel-Crafts acylation to **acetophenone**:

$$\ce{C6H5OH ->[Zn][\Delta] C6H6 (X') ->[CH3COCl/AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 (Y')}$$

**(b)** Propene is hydrated (Markovnikov) to **propan-2-ol**, which is oxidised by acidified dichromate to **propanone**:

$$\ce{CH3CH=CH2 ->[H3O^+] CH3CH(OH)CH3 (X') ->[K2Cr2O7/H^+] CH3COCH3 (Y')}$$

**(c)** Phenol with sodium gives **sodium phenoxide**, with hydrogen evolved:

$$\ce{2C6H5OH + 2Na -> 2C6H5ONa + H2 ^}$$

(X = sodium phenoxide.)
